misconceptions.label: Treats an ordered pair like an unordered set
misconceptions.description: The student thinks (a, b) is the same as (b, a), or the same as {a, b}, so they match components in the wrong positions.

refutation.text_md: You are treating the pair like a set, where only the numbers matter and the order does not. That is true for $\{a, b\}$, but not for an ordered pair $(a, b)$.

In an ordered pair, position carries meaning: the first place is the first projection and the second place is the second projection. Two ordered pairs are equal only when the first projections are equal and the second projections are equal.
Test it on $(a-2, b+1)=(2, -3)$. If you match crosswise, $a-2=-3$ and $b+1=2$ give $a=-1$ and $b=1$. Put these back: the left side is $(-3, 2)$, which is not $(2, -3)$.
Match by position. First projections: $a-2=2$, so $a=4$. Second projections: $b+1=-3$, so $b=-4$. Check: $(4-2, \,-4+1)=(2, -3)$.
Each time, first compare the two first places, then the two second places. Write one equation for each place.

misconceptions.label: Adds the sizes instead of multiplying
misconceptions.description: To find n(X×Y) or n(X²), the student adds (or doubles) the numbers of elements instead of multiplying n(X) by n(Y).

refutation.text_md: You found the right sizes, $n(Z)=3$, but then combined them by adding. Adding counts the elements of two sets put together. A cartesian product counts pairs.

Look at $Z^2$ with $Z=\{4, 5, -2\}$. Pair $4$ with each of the 3 elements, then pair $5$ with each of the 3, then $-2$ with each of the 3. That gives 3 groups of 3 pairs, which is $3\times 3=9$ pairs, not $3+3=6$.
The same applies to $X\times Z$ with $X=\{2, -1\}$ and $Z=\{4, 5, -2\}$. Each of the 2 elements of $X$ is paired with 3 elements of $Z$, so there are $2\times 3=6$ pairs, not $2+3=5$.
Use $n(X\times Y)=n(X)\times n(Y)$, and for a square $n(X^2)=n(X)\times n(X)$. A check is that $n(Y^2)=2\times 2=4$ for $Y=\{4, 0\}$ happens to equal $2+2$, so test your method on $Z^2$ as well.

The refutation's arithmetic is correct: Z² gives 3×3=9, X×Z gives 2×3=6, and Y²=4 coincides with 2+2. It argues against adding and does not just restate the method. misconceptions.label: Treats X×Y and Y×X as the same
misconceptions.description: The student writes the pairs with the elements in the wrong order, or assumes X×Y gives the same set as Y×X.

refutation.text_md: You have the right pairs of elements in mind, but you treated a pair like a set where order does not matter. In $X\times Y$ the first element of each pair must come from $X$ and the second from $Y$.
Take $X=\{a, b\}$ and $Y=\{-1, 0, 3\}$. Then $X\times Y$ contains $(a, -1)$, but $Y\times X$ contains $(-1, a)$. These are different ordered pairs, so $X\times Y\neq Y\times X$ when $X\neq Y$.

The same thing happens with $Y\times Z$ where $Y=\{4, 0\}$ and $Z=\{4, 5, -2\}$. The answer has pairs like $(4, 5)$ with a $Y$ element first. Writing $(5, 4)$ would put a $Z$ element first, and that belongs to $Z\times Y$.
Before you write each pair, check the order of the product. Take each element of the first set in turn and pair it with every element of the second set, always writing the first set's element first.

misconceptions.label: Accepts an element of X with two images
misconceptions.description: The student calls a relation a function even though one element of X is paired with more than one element of Y.

refutation.text_md: You may be checking that every pair is a sensible pair, or that every element of Y is used. That is not the test. The test is about the elements of X, and what comes out of each one.

Look at $\{(1, 10), (1, 12), (5, 10), (9, 12)\}$. The element $1$ is the first element of two pairs, $(1, 10)$ and $(1, 12)$. In an arrow diagram, two arrows would leave $1$, one to $10$ and one to $12$.

A function needs every element of X to have only one image, which means only one arrow coming out. Here $1$ has two images, so this relation is not a function. The other pairs being fine does not rescue it, because one element of X with two arrows is enough to fail.
Next time, take each element of X in turn and count the pairs that start with it, or the arrows that leave it. If any element has more than one, it is not a function.

misconceptions.label: Reads the degree from the unexpanded rule
misconceptions.description: The student takes the degree from the powers they see in the brackets or in the first terms, instead of expanding and simplifying first.

refutation.text_md: You looked at the powers of $x$ that are printed and picked the biggest. That works when the rule is already written as $a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_nx^n$, but brackets can hide what is left.

Take $f(x)=x(x-2x^2)$. The brackets show $x^2$, but multiplying out gives $x^2-2x^3$. The highest power is $3$, so the degree is $3$.
Next time, expand and simplify first, then read off the highest power of $x$ that is still there.

misconceptions.label: Counts 1/x or √x terms as allowed in a polynomial

misconceptions.label: Treats inverse variation as direct (y = mx, or the ratio turned the wrong way)
misconceptions.description: The student finds the constant by dividing y by x, or sets up y₁/y₂ = x₁/x₂, so y grows when x grows.

Inverse variation means $y \propto \frac{1}{x}$, so $y=\frac{m}{x}$, which is the same as $xy=m$. The constant is the product of x and y, not their quotient.
Test it with $y=3$ when $x=2$. Your way gives $m=1.5$ and then $y=1.5\times1.5=2.25$ at $x=1.5$. But x has got smaller, so y must get bigger than 3. 2.25 is smaller, so the method must be wrong.
The correct working is $3=\frac{m}{2}$, so $m=2\times3=6$. Then $y=\frac{6}{1.5}=4$, which is bigger than 3 as it should be.

Next time, write $y=\frac{m}{x}$ first, get $m$ by multiplying $x$ and $y$, and check that y moves the opposite way to x. With the ratio rule, remember it is $\frac{y_1}{y_2}=\frac{x_2}{x_1}$, with the x's turned over.

misconceptions.label: Reading m and b straight off the equation without isolating y
misconceptions.description: The student takes the number in front of $x$ as the slope, or the constant term as the y-intercept, without first writing the equation as $y = mx + b$.

Take $x - 2y + 4 = 0$. Here $y$ has coefficient $-2$, so the equation is not yet in that form. Rewrite it: $2y = x + 4$, then divide both sides by 2: $y = \frac{1}{2}x + 2$.
Now the slope is $\frac{1}{2}$ and the y-intercept is $2$. The numbers $1$ and $4$ you can see in the original equation were both still to be divided by 2.
You can check this against the graph. The line passes through $(0, 2)$, so the y-intercept is 2, not 4. Always get $y$ alone first, then read off $m$ and $b$.

misconceptions.label: Expects two lines to always meet at one point
misconceptions.description: The student assumes every pair of equations has exactly one solution and looks for a single intersection point even when the lines have equal slopes.

Take $3x + y = 4$ and $2y + 6x = 3$. Write them as $y = 4 - 3x$ and $y = \frac{3 - 6x}{2}$. The first passes through $(0, 4)$ and $(2, -2)$. The second passes through $(0, \frac{3}{2})$ and $(1, -\frac{3}{2})$.
Both lines have slope $-3$, so they go down at the same steepness. They stay the same distance apart and never meet, so $L_1 \cap L_2 = \phi$.
A solution has to lie on both lines. If the lines never meet, no point lies on both, so there is no solution.
Before you look for a crossing point, compare the slopes. Different slopes give one intersection point. Equal slopes mean the lines are parallel or coincide, and you must check which.

misconceptions.label: Calls parallel lines coincident
misconceptions.description: The student sees two lines with the same slope and decides they give infinitely many solutions, without checking whether they are the same line or different parallel lines.

Take $3x + y = 4$ and $2y + 6x = 3$. Both have slope $-3$. The first passes through $(0, 4)$ and the second through $(0, \frac{3}{2})$, so they are different lines.
Check the point $(0, 4)$ in the second equation: $2(4) + 6(0) = 8$, not $3$. A point on $L_1$ is not on $L_2$, so the lines never share a point and there is no solution.

Compare this with $3x + 2y = 6$ and $2y = 6 - 3x$. Rewriting the second gives $3x + 2y = 6$, which is exactly the first equation. Here every point of one line is on the other, so there are infinitely many solutions.

When the slopes match, put both equations in the same form. If they are identical, the lines coincide and there are infinitely many solutions. If only the constant differs, the lines are parallel and the solution set is empty.

misconceptions.label: Thinks two circles through A and B can meet at a third point

The center of every circle through $A$ and $B$ lies on the axis of the chord $AB$. Different centers on that axis give different circles, and all of them meet at $A$ and $B$.

Suppose a circle also went through a third point $C$. Its center would then lie on the axis of $AB$ and on the axis of the chord $AC$, and those two axes cross in only one point. So there is only one possible center and only one circle.
Two different circles therefore cannot intersect in more than two points. When two circles pass through $A$ and $B$, those two points are all they share.

The refutation uses the book's axis-of-chord idea (the center lies on the axis of any chord). A third common point C would force the center onto both the axis of AB and the axis of AC. Those axes meet in one point, so there is one circle. This is mathematically correct, consistent with the canonical answer No, and targets this error. It names no question ids, pages, figures or review history.

misconceptions.label: Equal means, so equally spread
misconceptions.description: The student finds that two sets have the same mean and concludes that their values are equally spread out, or that the sets are alike.
misconceptions.signal: Says two sets with the same mean have the same dispersion, without finding either range.

refutation.text_md: You found that both means are equal, and that part is right: both sets of wages have a mean of LE 200. The slip is in treating the mean as if it also told you how spread out the values are.
Look at the two sets of wages. Set A is $170, 180, 180, 230, 240$ and set B is $50, 180, 180, 190, 400$. Both add up to $1000$, so both have mean $200$.

But the values are not equally spread. Set A stays between $170$ and $240$, close to its mean. Set B runs from $50$ up to $400$, far on both sides of $200$. The mean is the same, yet B is clearly more scattered.
The mean tells you where the centre of the values is. It says nothing about how far the values stretch around that centre. Sets with the same mean can have very different spreads.
To compare dispersion, find the range of each set as greatest value $-$ smallest value. Compare the two ranges: the bigger range means the more divergent set.

Its closing step uses the book's range method, greatest minus smallest, and says the bigger range means the more divergent set. misconceptions.label: Thinks an event happens only when the outcome is the whole event set
misconceptions.description: The student treats an event like {2, 4, 6} as a single outcome that must come up as a whole, instead of seeing that the event occurs when the outcome is any one element of the set.

refutation.text_md: You are treating the event as one big outcome, so you think it only happens if the whole set turns up. It is natural to read $A = \{2, 4, 6\}$ as a single item, but it is a collection of outcomes.
A dice shows only one number per roll. If the whole set had to appear, the event 'getting an even number' could never happen, because one roll never shows 2, 4 and 6 together.

The book's rule is that an event occurred if the outcome of the experiment is an element of the set that expresses the event. If the dice shows 4, then 4 is in $\{2, 4, 6\}$, so the even-number event occurred.
This is also why we count elements: $P(A) = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)} = \frac{3}{6}$ counts the 3 outcomes that each make $A$ occur, out of the 6 possible outcomes.
Next time, ask 'Is the outcome one of the elements of the event set?' If yes, the event occurred. Then count those elements for $n(A)$.

provenance.verifier_reason: The book's caution says an event occurred if the outcome is an element of the event set. The error of treating the event as one outcome that must appear as a whole is a plausible reading of that caution. The refutation is mathematically correct: one roll shows one number, and a roll of 4 is in {2,4,6}. P(A)=3/6 matches the canonical n(A)/n(S). It cites no question ids, pages or figures, and it teaches nothing beyond the book.

misconceptions.label: Adds P(A) and P(B) and forgets the overlap
misconceptions.description: The student finds P(A ∪ B) by adding P(A) and P(B) even though the events share outcomes, so shared outcomes are counted twice.
misconceptions.signal: A probability for A ∪ B that is exactly P(A) + P(B), larger than the true value, when A and B overlap (e.g. 7/10 instead of 3/5, or 7/9 instead of 2/3).

refutation.text_md: You are thinking "A or B means add the two probabilities". That is right when A and B have nothing in common, and it is a good start. The trouble starts when they share an outcome.
Take cards numbered 1 to 9. $A$ is an even number, $A=\{2, 4, 6, 8\}$, so $P(A)=\frac{4}{9}$. $B$ is a number divisible by 3, $B=\{3, 6, 9\}$, so $P(B)=\frac{3}{9}$. Adding gives $\frac{7}{9}$.
Now list $A\cup B$ itself: $\{2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9\}$. That is only 6 cards, so $P(A\cup B)=\frac{6}{9}=\frac{2}{3}$, not $\frac{7}{9}$. The card 6 is in both $A$ and $B$, so adding counted it twice.
Take the shared outcomes away once: $A\cap B=\{6\}$, so $P(A\cap B)=\frac{1}{9}$, and $\frac{4}{9}+\frac{3}{9}-\frac{1}{9}=\frac{6}{9}=\frac{2}{3}$, which matches.
Next time, first find $A\cap B$. If it has outcomes in it, use $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. If $A\cap B$ is empty (mutually exclusive), the subtraction is $0$ and you just add.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real. Adding P(A) and P(B) gives 7/10 instead of 3/5 in drill (a), and 7/9 instead of 2/3 in the cards example. The refutation uses the book's own cards 1–9 example. Its numbers match the canonical solution: A={2,4,6,8}, B={3,6,9}, A∪B has 6 cards, P=2/3, and 4/9+3/9−1/9=2/3. It shows the double-count by listing A∪B directly, then applies the book's formula and the mutually exclusive case. It cites no question ids, pages or figures, and no review history.

misconceptions.label: Counts the whole set A when asked for A only
misconceptions.description: The student takes the 'only' event A - B to be the whole set A, so they use all of A's students and never remove the overlap A ∩ B.
misconceptions.signal: Gives 18/40 (or 9/20) for reading Al-Akhbar only, or 15/40 (or 3/8) for Al-Ahram only.

refutation.text_md: You are treating 'reads Al-Akhbar' and 'reads Al-Akhbar only' as the same event. You were right to start from the 18 students in set A.

Those 18 students are made of two groups. Some read only Al-Akhbar. Others read Al-Akhbar and Al-Ahram too, and that second group is the 8 in $A \cap B$. This is what $(A - B) \cup (A \cap B) = A$ says.
The 8 students who read both also read Al-Ahram, so they do not belong to 'Al-Akhbar only'. Answering $\frac{18}{40}$ counts them as well.
Take the overlap away: $n(A - B) = 18 - 8 = 10$, so $P(A - B) = \frac{10}{40} = \frac{1}{4}$, not $\frac{18}{40}$.
Whenever a question says 'only', subtract the overlap first: $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$. Then divide by $n(S)$.
